name: Cannabis / CBD for sleep

card.summary: Cannabis and cannabidiol are used for sleep onset, but clinical evidence is limited and CBD supplements are not FDA-approved for sleep.
card.note: CBD products are often mislabeled; FDA has raised liver, drug-interaction and fertility concerns.

quick.overview:
Some people use cannabis products or cannabidiol (CBD) to fall asleep. Wikipedia's CBD article says clinical evidence for sleep benefit is limited, and lists sleepiness as a common effect and insomnia among adverse effects of the approved drug Epidiolex.

Only small trials have been registered, for example a phase 2 study of cannabinoids for insomnia in major depression with 14 participants.
quick.mechanism: CBD is a non-intoxicating cannabis constituent whose sleep-related mechanisms remain unestablished in the sources reviewed here. THC is the main intoxicating compound.
quick.risks: The FDA has cited possible liver toxicity, drug interactions, effects on mood and alertness, and unknown long-term effects. FDA studies found many CBD products were inaccurately labeled and about half of 147 tested contained THC. Legal status varies widely.

lead: Cannabis products and cannabidiol (CBD) are used by some people to fall asleep more easily. In appearance terms the chain is sleep-based: people who sleep longer and more regularly say they look fresher, carry less under-eye darkness and recover better from training, so a product that helps them fall asleep is seen as supporting those looks goals indirectly.

CBD is a non-intoxicating cannabis constituent, while THC is the main intoxicating one. The only FDA-approved CBD medicine, Epidiolex (2018), is indicated for certain seizure disorders, not sleep.[1] Wikipedia notes that CBD may help with pain, sleep and addiction according to some claims, that clinical evidence is limited, and that somnolence is a common effect.[1]

Research on cannabis and sleep is mixed. A 2023 randomised crossover trial in adults with insomnia tested a medicinal cannabis oil against placebo and reported improved sleep, while a 2025 meta-analysis of polysomnography studies found cannabis does not consistently change sleep duration, latency or staging, and that withdrawal from regular use is associated with sleep disturbance.[3][4]
infobox: Varies; hemp-derived CBD with 0.3% THC or less is unscheduled federally in the US [1]
Mixed results in trials and meta-analyses [3][4]

paras: Users take cannabis by smoking, vaping or edibles, and CBD as oils, gummies or hemp flower, often in the evening.[5][6] On T Nation, one poster described using a high-CBD edible alongside a calming supplement and said it worked well for sleep, while another asked what CBD oil actually does and noted that it is heavily hyped.[5][6]

CBD side effects are dose-related and include somnolence, sedation, fatigue, diarrhea and appetite changes [1]. The FDA has raised concerns about liver toxicity, interactions with prescription drugs, gastrointestinal problems and effects on alertness and mood, and in later updates about long-term effects, pregnancy and male fertility [1].
Product quality studies found labeling problems: a 2017 analysis of online US products found 69% mislabeled, and a 2020 FDA study of 147 products found half contained THC [1].
A 2024 review of cannabis harms in the Annual Review of Medicine covers health risks of use more broadly.[8]

A 2023 double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of a medicinal cannabis oil in 29 adults with self-reported insomnia reported improved sleep over six weeks, as indicated by its title.[3] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 polysomnography studies (nine in the meta-analysis) found no consistent change in sleep duration, latency, wake time, efficiency or stages with cannabis administration, noted that early REM-suppression findings came from small high-THC studies, and found withdrawal consistently associated with shorter sleep and longer sleep onset.[4]
A phase 2 trial of cannabinoids for insomnia in major depression (n=14) was completed in 2023; no results are reported in its registry entry.[2]

timeline.event: Structure and stereochemistry of CBD determined [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, cannabis and CBD come up as sleep aids and as part of broader questions about how substance use affects looks and health.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Cannabis or CBD helps you fall asleep
claims.believers: T Nation posters report good results from high-CBD edibles or hemp flower for sleep, while others note that CBD is hyped.[5][6]
claims.experts: A 2023 crossover trial reported improved sleep with a medicinal cannabis oil, while a 2025 meta-analysis found no consistent change in sleep parameters.[3][4]

claims.claim: Withdrawal after regular use can worsen sleep
claims.believers: Forum users discuss returning to cannabis after stopping and weigh it against nicotine for health and looks.[7]
claims.experts: The 2025 meta-analysis found withdrawal from active use consistently associated with reduced total sleep and longer sleep onset.[4]

claims.claim: CBD products are what the label says
claims.believers: Sellers market CBD widely for sleep and calm.[1]
claims.experts: A 2017 analysis found most sampled online products mislabeled, and a 2020 FDA study found about half of 147 products contained THC.[1]

angle.text: People use cannabis or CBD products at night hoping to fall asleep faster, and better sleep is widely linked in the community with a rested face and better training recovery. The effect on sleep itself varies by product and person in the research.
